title: Year 9 Chemistry: Periodic Table, separation and RP6

questions.prompt: Who made an early list that included some substances later found not to be elements?
questions.hint: Recall who made the early list, before Newlands and Mendeleev.

questions.prompt: Newlands arranged elements in increasing order of what?
questions.hint: Newlands used mass; the modern table uses atomic number.

questions.prompt: Under Newlands’ Law of Octaves, similar properties recurred at which interval?
questions.hint: Count the repeating pattern to the eighth element.

questions.prompt: Which problem occurred in Newlands’ table?
options: Very different elements were placed together.

accepted: Very different elements were placed together.

questions.hint: Think about why a group should contain chemically similar elements.

questions.prompt: Mendeleev arranged elements mainly by which property?
questions.hint: Mendeleev mainly used mass, then adjusted placement by properties.

questions.prompt: Mendeleev grouped elements with similar what?
questions.hint: A group should show similar reactions and chemical behaviour.

questions.prompt: What did Mendeleev deliberately leave for undiscovered elements?
questions.hint: Undiscovered elements need spaces to fit later.

questions.prompt: Why did Mendeleev swap the order of some elements?
options: To keep elements with similar properties together.
To fit the Law of Octaves.

accepted: To keep elements with similar properties together.

questions.hint: Use chemical behaviour to decide grouping, even if mass order changes.

questions.prompt: The modern Periodic Table orders elements by increasing what?
questions.hint: Atomic number means the number of protons.

questions.prompt: Which method separates an insoluble solid such as sand from water?
questions.hint: Ask whether the solid dissolves before choosing a separation method.

questions.prompt: In filtration, what is the solid left on the paper called?
questions.hint: Residue remains; filtrate passes through.

questions.prompt: What is the liquid that passes through filter paper called?
questions.hint: Filtrate flows through; residue stays on the filter.

questions.prompt: Which method leaves a soluble solid behind by removing the solvent?
questions.hint: Evaporation leaves solute but does not collect solvent.

questions.prompt: Which method grows pure crystals from a solution after partial evaporation and cooling?
questions.hint: Cool a concentrated solution to grow crystals.

questions.prompt: Which method collects a solvent from a solution by boiling and condensing it?
questions.hint: Collect the vapour after it condenses.

questions.prompt: Which method uses a fractionating column to separate miscible liquids?
questions.hint: The column separates liquids through repeated boiling and condensation.

questions.prompt: Salt is insoluble in ethanol while sugar dissolves. What should be added first to separate them?
questions.hint: Use the solvent in which only sugar dissolves.

questions.prompt: After dissolving sugar in ethanol, which method separates the undissolved salt?
questions.hint: Filter after dissolving one component.

questions.prompt: After filtration, where is the salt?
options: on the filter paper as residue

accepted: on the filter paper as residue

questions.hint: Track what dissolves and what stays solid.

questions.prompt: How can the sugar be recovered from the ethanol filtrate?
questions.hint: Remove the ethanol from the filtrate to recover sugar.

questions.prompt: What should be used to draw the start line?
questions.hint: Use a material that cannot dissolve and create an extra spot.

questions.prompt: Why use pencil rather than ink?
options: Pencil does not dissolve in the solvent.

accepted: Pencil does not dissolve in the solvent.

questions.hint: Explain both the cause and its effect on the chromatogram.

questions.prompt: Where must the start line be relative to the solvent level?
options: at the bottom of the beaker
questions.hint: The start line must stay out of the solvent.

questions.prompt: Why keep the spots small?
questions.hint: Large spots can smear together.

questions.prompt: When should the solvent front be marked?
questions.hint: The front can disappear as the solvent evaporates.

questions.prompt: Why mark the solvent front immediately?
questions.hint: Mark before it evaporates, then measure accurately.

questions.prompt: Figure 1: Which start-line error is shown?
options: It is too high above the solvent.
questions.hint: Look closely at what made the line.

questions.prompt: Figure 1: What effect can the ink start line have?
options: It may dissolve and interfere with the results.

accepted: It may dissolve and interfere with the results.

questions.hint: Explain what happens to the ink itself.

questions.prompt: Figure 1: Where are the sample spots relative to the solvent?
questions.hint: Compare the spot height with the liquid level.

questions.prompt: Figure 1: What could happen to spots below the solvent?
options: They may dissolve into the beaker solvent and wash off.

accepted: They may dissolve into the beaker solvent and wash off.

questions.hint: What happens when the sample starts in the solvent?

questions.prompt: Figure 1: What is wrong with the position of the paper?
options: It is too short to reach solvent.
questions.hint: Check whether the paper has a clear gap from the beaker wall.

questions.prompt: What can happen when paper touches the beaker wall?
questions.hint: Uneven solvent rise distorts the spots.

questions.prompt: Figure 2: Which inks are mixtures?
questions.hint: Count spots in each labelled column.

questions.prompt: Figure 2: Which inks are single dyes?
questions.hint: One spot suggests one dye under these conditions.

questions.prompt: Figure 2: What observation shows B is a mixture?
options: It is on the start line.
questions.hint: Count the distinct spots above B.

questions.prompt: Figure 2: Which coloured spot is most soluble in this solvent?

feedback.short: The yellow spot travelled furthest towards the solvent front.

questions.hint: The most soluble spot travels furthest in this solvent.

questions.prompt: Figure 3: What is the solvent-front distance travelled from the start line, in mm?

feedback.short: The solvent front is at 50 mm on a scale measured from the start line.

questions.hint: Subtract the start-line reading from the front reading.

questions.prompt: Figure 3: What distance did the blue dye travel from the start line, in mm?

feedback.short: Read to the centre of the spot: 30 mm from the start line.

questions.hint: Measure to the centre of the spot, from the start line.

questions.prompt: Figure 3: Calculate Rf for the blue dye (no unit).
questions.hint: Rf = dye distance ÷ solvent-front distance.

questions.prompt: Figure 3: Which reference dye matches an Rf of 0.60?

feedback.short: This matches the reference value for green under the same conditions.

questions.hint: Use the Rf reference value, not the visible spot colour alone.

questions.prompt: Figure 4: Which solvent separated the three dyes more clearly?
questions.hint: Compare how well the spots are separated.

questions.prompt: Figure 4: What evidence supports that choice?
options: The spots are more spread out and distinct.

accepted: The spots are more spread out and distinct.

questions.hint: Use spread and overlap as the evidence.

questions.prompt: What does one spot from a sample usually suggest?
options: It is pure or contains one dye.
It is insoluble in all solvents.

accepted: It is pure or contains one dye.

questions.hint: State the observation and what it means.

questions.prompt: Name one advantage of gas chromatography over paper chromatography.

feedback.short: It can detect smaller amounts and separate complex mixtures precisely.

questions.hint: Gas chromatography can detect smaller quantities.

questions.prompt: How can an unknown dye be identified from a chromatogram?
options: Compare its Rf with known dyes under the same conditions.
Compare only the colour of the beaker.
Use any solvent without recording it.

accepted: Compare its Rf with known dyes under the same conditions.

questions.hint: Compare with known dyes under the same solvent and conditions.

questions.prompt: A newly discovered element behaves like the elements in a particular group. Which feature of Mendeleev’s table made room for it?
questions.hint: Link the prediction to empty spaces in the table.

questions.prompt: An element’s mass order would put it beside unlike elements. What would Mendeleev prioritise?
questions.hint: Chemical behaviour determined the group.

questions.prompt: What modern quantity fixes the position of an element more reliably than relative atomic mass?
questions.hint: Atomic number counts protons.

questions.prompt: Newlands sometimes placed two different elements in one space. What is this best classified as?
questions.hint: Recall a criticism of Newlands, not a feature of Mendeleev.

questions.prompt: Later discovery of an element with predicted properties would support whose table?
questions.hint: Gaps and predictions are associated with Mendeleev.

questions.prompt: Which scientist proposed a repeating pattern every eighth element?
questions.hint: The name of the pattern is Law of Octaves.

questions.prompt: A beaker contains sand and dissolved salt. Which step removes sand first?
questions.hint: Filter the insoluble component first.

questions.prompt: After removing sand, how could you collect the water from the salt solution?
questions.hint: If you need the solvent, it must be condensed and collected.

questions.prompt: Why is crystallisation preferable when strong heating might decompose the solute?
options: all liquids have one boiling point
questions.hint: Allow crystals to form on cooling.

questions.prompt: Oil fractions have different boiling ranges. Which equipment is central to their separation?
questions.hint: Think of repeated vaporisation and condensation.

questions.prompt: Copper sulfate is dissolved in water. What is the dissolved substance called?
questions.hint: Distinguish solute from solvent.

questions.prompt: The condensed liquid collected after distillation is called the…
questions.hint: This is the collected condensed vapour.

questions.prompt: Why would filtering a mixture of dissolved salt and dissolved sugar in water fail?
questions.hint: Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid.

questions.prompt: The student uses a large blob of ink at the start line. What is the likely result?
questions.hint: The starting spots should be small.

questions.prompt: At which point should the distance of a dye spot be measured?
questions.hint: Measure from the start line to its centre.

questions.prompt: Why use the same solvent when comparing an unknown dye with a reference?
questions.hint: Changing conditions can change Rf.

questions.prompt: A student forgets to mark the solvent front. Which measurement becomes unreliable?
questions.hint: The front may evaporate and become invisible.

questions.prompt: Figure 1: Which one change would stop the sample spots washing into the solvent?
options: lower the solvent level below the spots

accepted: lower the solvent level below the spots

questions.hint: The spots must begin above the liquid level.

questions.prompt: Figure 1: Which improvement prevents uneven solvent movement at the paper edge?
options: keep paper away from beaker wall

accepted: keep paper away from beaker wall

questions.hint: Inspect the paper’s right edge.

questions.prompt: Figure 1: If the blue ink start line dissolves, what could appear?
questions.hint: The line itself may travel and contaminate the result.

questions.prompt: Figure 2: How many components are shown in ink D?
questions.hint: Count the spots vertically above D.

questions.prompt: Figure 2: Why is A described as one dye under these conditions?
questions.hint: Count the spots above A.

questions.prompt: Figure 2: Which labelled ink has three distinct components?
questions.hint: Look at the column with purple, blue and green.

questions.prompt: Figure 3: If the dye travels 30 mm and the solvent travels 50 mm, which division gives Rf?
questions.hint: The substance distance is the numerator.

questions.prompt: Figure 3: Why is an Rf of 0.60 written without mm?
options: it is a ratio with no unit

accepted: it is a ratio with no unit

questions.hint: The same distance units cancel.

questions.prompt: A spot travels 24 mm and the solvent front 40 mm. Calculate Rf.
questions.hint: Divide the spot distance by the solvent distance.

questions.prompt: A dye has Rf 0.45 in the same solvent as a reference dye of Rf 0.45. What is the cautious conclusion?
options: they may be the same dye

accepted: they may be the same dye

questions.hint: Matching Rf supports identity but is not absolute proof.

questions.prompt: Figure 4: In ethanol, the three spots are close together. What does that imply?
questions.hint: Compare distinctness of spots across the two papers.

questions.prompt: A new solvent spreads previously overlapping spots apart. What improved?
questions.hint: More distinct spots make components easier to identify.

questions.prompt: Which observation supports the claim that an unknown ink is a mixture?
questions.hint: State the observation before the conclusion.

questions.prompt: Why is an Rf comparison alone insufficient if one test uses ethanol and the other water?
questions.hint: Keep conditions the same for identification.

questions.prompt: One advantage of gas chromatography is detecting very small quantities. What is this called?
questions.hint: Choose the analytical word for a low detection limit.

questions.prompt: Teacher-style setup: a start line is drawn in ink. Which consequence earns the explanation mark?
options: The ink dissolves and interferes with the chromatogram.
It raises the solvent front accurately.

accepted: The ink dissolves and interferes with the chromatogram.

questions.hint: Pair the mistake with the effect. Naming the mistake alone would miss the explanation mark.

questions.prompt: Teacher-style setup: sample spots begin under the solvent level. Which consequence earns the explanation mark?
options: Samples dissolve into the solvent and may wash off.

accepted: Samples dissolve into the solvent and may wash off.

questions.hint: Link the level to loss of sample.

questions.prompt: Teacher-style chromatogram: what does the black sample contain?
questions.hint: Count the separated black spots, then state what that means.

questions.prompt: Teacher-style chromatogram: which known colours align with spots in the black mixture?
questions.hint: Compare horizontal spot positions under the same solvent.

questions.prompt: Teacher-style chromatogram: why is the black sample described as a mixture?
options: It begins at the start line.
questions.hint: The observation is the number of spots, not the original colour.

questions.prompt: Teacher-style chromatogram: sample B remains at the start line. What does this suggest in this solvent?
options: It did not travel with the solvent.
It must be the same as D.
It contains all three black dyes.

accepted: It did not travel with the solvent.

questions.hint: Look for movement from the baseline.

questions.prompt: Teacher-style calculation: a spot travels 45 mm and the solvent front 74 mm. Which Rf is closest?
questions.hint: Substance distance goes on top. Round to two decimal places.

questions.prompt: Teacher-style reference table: a measured Rf of 0.61 matches which food colour?
questions.hint: Match the calculated Rf to the reference under the same solvent.

questions.prompt: Teacher-style reference table: which conclusion is supported by Rf 0.40 in the same solvent?
options: It is necessarily a pure mixture.
No comparison is possible in the same solvent.
questions.hint: Use cautious wording: matching Rf suggests identity.

questions.prompt: Teacher-style 1-mark question: which is a valid advantage of gas chromatography?
options: It uses an ink start line.
questions.hint: One clear advantage is enough for one mark.

questions.prompt: A newly found element fills a gap in Mendeleev’s table. Its measured properties closely match his earlier prediction. What makes this stronger evidence than simply finding a new element?

accepted: The measured properties matched Mendeleev’s prediction.

questions.modelAnswer: The measured properties matched Mendeleev’s prediction.
questions.hint: Compare a prediction made before discovery with what was observed.

questions.prompt: Two elements have similar reaction patterns but their relative atomic masses seem to put them apart. Which evidence would support placing them in the same group?

accepted: Their similar chemical properties support grouping them together.

questions.modelAnswer: Their similar chemical properties support grouping them together.
questions.hint: A group is meant to reflect chemical behaviour.

questions.prompt: A mixture contains sand, dissolved salt and water. You need to collect clean water and keep the sand. Name the first separation step and the later step that collects the water.

accepted: Filter out the sand, then distil the salt solution to collect water.

questions.modelAnswer: Filter out the sand, then distil the salt solution to collect water.
questions.hint: First remove the insoluble solid; then boil and condense the solvent.

questions.prompt: Two miscible liquids have close boiling points. Explain why a fractionating column helps separate them better than simple distillation.

accepted: The column causes repeated evaporation and condensation, enriching the lower-boiling liquid in the vapour.

questions.modelAnswer: The column causes repeated evaporation and condensation, enriching the lower-boiling liquid in the vapour.
questions.hint: Describe what happens inside the column.

questions.prompt: A heat-sensitive solute is dissolved in water. A student boils the solution to dryness. What change would allow crystals to form while reducing the chance of decomposition?

required: evaporate some water and leave to cool
make a saturated solution then cool
accepted: Gently evaporate some water, then allow the concentrated solution to cool and crystallise.

questions.modelAnswer: Gently evaporate some water, then allow the concentrated solution to cool and crystallise.
questions.hint: Do not heat the solid to dryness.

questions.prompt: An unknown ink and a reference dye are run on separate chromatography papers. Why is it better to run them on the same paper with the same solvent?

accepted: They experience the same conditions, making spot positions or Rf values more comparable.

questions.modelAnswer: They experience the same conditions, making spot positions or Rf values more comparable.
questions.hint: Think about what must be controlled before comparing positions.

questions.prompt: A student repeats the chromatogram three times and obtains Rf values 0.42, 0.43 and 0.41. What quality of the method does this agreement show?

accepted: Repeatability: repeats with the same method produced similar results.

questions.modelAnswer: Repeatability: repeats with the same method produced similar results.
questions.hint: Similar repeated measurements support this term.

questions.prompt: A student places the start line below the solvent surface. State the change to the method that keeps sample spots on the paper at the start.

accepted: Place the pencil start line and sample spots above the solvent level.

questions.modelAnswer: Place the pencil start line and sample spots above the solvent level.
questions.hint: The spots must not begin immersed.

questions.prompt: An unknown dye matches a reference Rf in ethanol, but their spots do not match when both are run again in water. Why is the first match alone insufficient to prove identity?

accepted: A single matching Rf is not proof of identity; the different result in water argues against a secure match.

questions.modelAnswer: A single matching Rf is not proof of identity; the different result in water argues against a secure match.
questions.hint: A numerical match under one condition can occur by chance.

questions.prompt: A ruler shows the start line at 8 mm, the dye centre at 44 mm and the solvent front at 68 mm. Calculate the Rf value to two decimal places.

feedback.short: Subtract the start-line reading from both: (44−8) ÷ (68−8) = 36 ÷ 60 = 0.60.

questions.hint: Subtract the start-line reading from both measurements before dividing.

questions.prompt: A pupil calculates Rf = 1.25 for a spot that remained below the solvent front. What does this result tell you about the pupil’s calculation?

accepted: The calculation or distances are wrong: a spot below the solvent front has Rf below 1.

questions.modelAnswer: The calculation or distances are wrong: a spot below the solvent front has Rf below 1.
questions.hint: Compare how far the spot and solvent each travelled.

questions.prompt: A sample gives one spot on a paper chromatogram. Can the student conclude with certainty that it contains only one substance? Give the limitation.

required: different substances may have same rf
accepted: No. More than one substance could overlap or fail to separate in this solvent.

questions.modelAnswer: No. More than one substance could overlap or fail to separate in this solvent.
questions.hint: One visible spot is evidence under these conditions, not absolute proof.

questions.prompt: In solvent A, three dyes travel 18, 19 and 20 mm; in solvent B, they travel 8, 25 and 42 mm. Which solvent better resolves the mixture?

feedback.short: Its spots are farther apart: 8, 25 and 42 mm compared with 18, 19 and 20 mm.

questions.hint: Compare the spacing of the three spots.
